title: Were U.S. citizens in Japanese internment camps?
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss the U.S. incarceration of Japanese and Japanese Americans during World War II, opening with a riff on a Magnum P.I. episode set in a camp on Sand Island and a Simpsons reference. They cover Pearl Harbor, Executive Order 9066, the roundup of enemy aliens (including Italians and Germans) and Japanese Canadians, the assembly centers and ten relocation camps run by the War Relocation Authority, living conditions, the loyalty questionnaire and the Tule Lake protest and renunciations, the Korematsu case, the closing of the camps, and the Aleut (Unangax) internment at Killisnoo and other sites in Alaska. They also cover the Commission on Wartime Relocation's findings, the 1988 Civil Liberties Act, reparations, and the official apology. The episode ends with a listener mail update on Sergeant John Walker's recovery after being shot in Afghanistan.

segments.title: Opening banter and Magnum P.I. Sand Island episode
segments.summary: Hosts banter about Simpsons and a season three Magnum P.I. episode set in a Japanese internment camp on Sand Island, then introduce the topic of U.S. citizens interned during World War II.

segments.title: Pearl Harbor, enemy alien roundups, and Executive Order 9066
segments.summary: After Pearl Harbor, about fifteen hundred aliens were rounded up on suspicion of espionage, including Italians, Germans and Japanese, and about twenty thousand people in Canada were also detained. Executive Order 9066 let the military create exclusion zones, and Japanese residents were effectively forced out of them.

segments.title: Assembly centers and forced sale of property
segments.summary: Japanese and Japanese Americans from the West Coast were given only a couple of weeks to leave homes and report to temporary assembly centers. Government-enlisted lawyers helped them sell homes and businesses, often at a loss. A propaganda film of the era is mentioned.

segments.title: Life inside the relocation camps
segments.summary: The War Relocation Authority ran ten camps in states including California, Arizona, Colorado, Idaho, Utah, Wyoming, Arkansas, and Hawaii. Camps were guarded and barbed-wired, with barracks offering little privacy, shared bathrooms and mess halls, low wages that eroded parental authority, and baseball leagues and family life disrupted.

segments.title: Loyalty questionnaire and Tule Lake protest
segments.summary: In 1943 the War Relocation Authority issued a questionnaire used to decide releases, including questions about loyalty and denouncing the Emperor of Japan. About seven thousand of the 112,000 people relocated were American citizens. Some refused to sign, and a mass protest took place at Tule Lake, where some renounced citizenship; Jimmy Omura is discussed, and citizenship was later restored.

segments.title: Camp closures, Korematsu-era legal challenges, and financial losses
segments.summary: The camps closed in late 1944 after public outcry, but returning internees often found property taken or ruined, with losses estimated at hundreds of millions of dollars. Mitsuye Endo's habeas corpus case reached the Supreme Court, which ordered her release, opening the way for other citizens to be freed.

segments.title: Sand Island deaths and Aleut internment in Alaska
segments.summary: An artist's work at the Renwick Gallery depicted a deaf old man shot by a guard in a camp. The hosts then describe the internment of Unangax (Aleut) people from the Aleutian Islands after fears of a Japanese invasion, including poor conditions at former fish and mining sites, where many died. Twenty-five men later joined the U.S. armed forces.

segments.title: Commission findings, reparations, and apology
segments.summary: Congress created the Commission on Wartime Relocation in 1980, which found the internment was caused by racism and wartime hysteria. About 82,210 people received twenty thousand dollars each, and the 1988 Civil Liberties Act added further payments, an official apology, and landmark status for the camp sites, along with an educational foundation.

segments.title: Listener mail: Sergeant John Walker update
segments.summary: A listener email from Sergeant John Walker, shot in Afghanistan, describes his coma and recovery, his promotion, medals, plans to serve another tour and then join law enforcement, and thanks listeners for support.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close with a request for beach stories and a reminder about the website and app.
